442.title: An audience of one
442.hook: enough are few, enough is one, enough is none
442.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism try to do their work well regardless of how many will see it, treating a single person, or no one, as audience enough.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the crowd, which shapes us more than we notice. Your line was what I bring home.

A post gets four likes and you feel faintly foolish for sharing it. A song you worked on for months gets a hundred plays. A talk you prepared gets a half-empty room. There's a number under nearly everything we make now. Seneca didn't have the number, but he knew the itch. Right after warning Lucilius about the crowd, he ends his seventh letter with three small sayings about how big an audience really needs to be.
screen: `FOUR LIKES.` → `A HALF-EMPTY ROOM.` → `AN AUDIENCE OF ONE.`

segments.voice: Lucilius might object: then what did I learn all this for, if no one will hear it? Seneca's first answer: you learned it for yourself. Then he gives three sayings, like three small gifts. First, Democritus, the old philosopher of atoms: one person counts as much as a whole people to me, and a whole people as much as one. The size of the audience doesn't change the worth of the work. Second, a craftsman, though Seneca says it's uncertain who. Asked why he took such pains over an art very few would ever appreciate, he answered: a few are enough for me. One is enough. None is enough. The work was worth doing well for its own sake. Third, Epicurus, the founder of a rival school, writing to a friend who studied with him: I say this not for the many, but for you; we are each a big enough audience for the other. Seneca's point, gathering all three: don't let the pleasure of being praised by many pull you back into the crowd. Most of the good in the world is done for an audience of one: a meal for a sick friend, a letter, a careful repair, a child's question answered properly. Nobody counts those. They count anyway.

segments.voice: Picture one person who will benefit from something you do today: a coworker, a parent, a kid with homework, a patient, a neighbor. See their face, and picture doing that one thing really well, as if they were the whole audience, because they are. Let that be enough.

443.title: All mine is with me
443.hook: Stilpo lost city, wife and children and said everything of his was still with him
443.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism reflect on which of their goods are truly their own, character, judgment, kindness, so that losses elsewhere do not take away their footing.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Democritus, for whom one listener counted as a whole people. Your line was one is enough.

A city has just fallen. The conqueror, a king called Demetrius, nicknamed the Besieger of Cities, has taken Megara. Houses are wrecked, goods carried off, families scattered. Somewhere in the ruins stands a philosopher named Stilpo, whose home is gone and whose wife and children are lost to him. The king asks him: have you lost anything? Seneca tells the story, and Stilpo's answer, in his ninth letter.
screen: `MEGARA HAS FALLEN.` → `HAVE YOU LOST ANYTHING?` → `ALL MINE IS WITH ME.`

segments.voice: Stilpo told the king: I have all my goods with me. He meant his true goods, Seneca explains, the kind no hand can seize. What was scattered, wrecked and carried off he didn't count as his own, only as things that had come to him from outside. It's fair to flinch at this. Losing a family is not a small thing, and Seneca doesn't say it is. In the same letter he says the wise person feels their troubles, and then overcomes them. Not numb. Not untouched. Still standing. The surprise is where Seneca puts the story: in a letter about friendship. Lucilius has asked whether someone complete in themselves needs friends at all. Seneca says the wise person is content with themselves, and can live without friends if they must, but still wants them, very much. Not to have someone who'll sit at their bedside, but to have someone at whose bedside they can sit. So Stilpo's line isn't a reason to love less. Read this way, it's a reason to love without fear. If what's most yours can't be taken, you can give your heart to people and things freely, knowing that even if you lose them, you won't lose yourself. In Seneca's Latin: omnia mea mecum sunt. All mine is with me.

444.title: As if seen
444.hook: live among people as if God saw you, speak to God as if people heard
444.carry: the private and public self become one
444.howItsDone: Some people, religious and not, try to act in private as they would before a kind and clear-eyed witness, so that their private and public lives match.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Stilpo, who kept his true goods in fallen Megara. Your line was you won't lose yourself.

Behind a closed door, where nobody will ever know, small choices get made: whether to return the extra change, whether to read the message over someone's shoulder, whether to say the unkind thing in a private chat. The person making them isn't always the one the world sees. Seneca's tenth letter is about being alone, and it ends with a sentence that closes the gap between the two versions of a person, from both directions.
screen: `WHEN THE DOOR IS CLOSED.` → `TWO SLIGHTLY DIFFERENT PEOPLE.` → `AS IF SEEN.`

segments.voice: It starts with a warning. Crates the Cynic saw a young man walking by himself and asked what he was doing out there alone. I'm talking with myself, the young man said. Crates answered: be careful, then, you're talking with a bad man. Solitude is only good, Seneca says, if the company inside is good. Then he passes on a saying of Athenodorus: you'll know you're free of your cravings when you ask God for nothing you couldn't ask for openly, in front of everyone. Seneca notes how many people whisper prayers they'd be ashamed for others to hear. And then his own line: live among people as if God were watching; speak with God as if people were listening. Two directions. With others, act as you would before the highest witness you know. Alone with the highest, ask only for what you'd be glad to have heard. Seneca says God here. Listeners of any faith may hear that word in their own way, and those without one can think of the best witness they can imagine. A life lived as if seen, by someone kind and clear-eyed, doesn't need two versions. The person behind the closed door and the person in the crowd can finally be the same.

445.title: Choose a Cato
445.hook: pick someone good and live as if they were watching
445.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a chosen model in mind, a person of good character, and ask in hard moments what that person would see in their choices.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Athenodorus: ask for nothing you couldn't ask openly. Your line was the private and public self become one.

When you're stuck on something, a hard conversation, a temptation, a choice at work, there's a question people reach for: what would she do? My grandmother. My old coach. The best boss I ever had. Some people keep a name on a bracelet for just that moment. The move is old. Yesterday Seneca said to live as if God saw you. In his eleventh letter he makes it more human and more specific, with advice borrowed, once again, from Epicurus.
screen: `WHAT WOULD SHE DO?` → `A NAME ON A BRACELET.` → `CHOOSE A CATO.`

segments.voice: The letter starts with a young friend of Lucilius who blushed while talking to Seneca. Seneca liked him for it. Blushing is natural, he says, and no amount of wisdom removes it. Actors can fake tears or fear on stage, but they can't blush on command. Some things in us we can't control; character is about what we do with the rest. Then the advice. Epicurus told his students to pick a person of good character and keep them always before their eyes, living as if that person were watching and acting as if that person could see. A guardian, Seneca calls it, a witness you carry with you. Choose a Cato, he says. Cato the Younger was the stern Roman Stoic who refused to bend to Julius Caesar and died rather than submit. If Cato feels too severe, choose Laelius, a gentler man, a statesman known as the Wise. Choose someone whose life, words and even face have pleased you. Why does it work? You can't straighten something crooked without a ruler. We need a measure outside ourselves to see where we bend. Your Cato doesn't have to be famous, or Roman, or even alive: a grandmother, a saint, a teacher, a neighbor. Just someone whose goodness you're sure of, and whose imagined gaze makes you stand a little straighter.

446.title: The old plane trees
446.hook: at his country house Seneca finds the trees he planted grown old, and so is he
446.howItsDone: Readers of Seneca's twelfth letter often take it as an invitation to notice their own aging with humor and affection rather than complaint.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Cato, a good person kept before your eyes. Your line was stand a little straighter.

Seneca goes out to his house in the country. The walls are cracking, and he scolds the man who manages the place: what are you spending the money on? The manager says, very politely, that it isn't his fault. The house is old. Seneca walks on, a little irritated, to the plane trees by the path, and finds them bare and knotted. Has nobody been looking after these? The manager swears he's been digging and watering them. And then Seneca remembers who planted them.
screen: `A CRACKING COUNTRY HOUSE.` → `BARE, KNOTTED TREES.` → `THE OLD PLANE TREES.`

segments.voice: Wherever he turns, Seneca says at the start of letter twelve, he sees signs of his age. The house is crumbling, and he built it. The plane trees are gnarled, their branches twisted and dry, and he planted them himself and saw their first leaves. The trees are simply old. So, Seneca realizes, is he. Then at the door he sees a frail old man and asks, rather rudely, who on earth that is. The old man answers: don't you know me? I'm Felicio, the son of your old manager. You used to bring me little toys. I was your favorite. Seneca, who wrote this himself, lets the joke land on him. Everything he complains about, he's part of. And then, instead of sinking, he turns. Let us welcome old age and love it, he says. It's full of pleasure if you know how to use it. Fruit tastes best just as the season ends. Youth is loveliest near its close. The last drink is the one the drinker savors. Every age has its own sweetness, and the late one has a kind all its own. Seneca and his trees, Seneca and Felicio, the house and the man who built it: not a tragedy. A shared life.

segments.voice: Look around for something that has aged alongside you: a chair, a book with a cracked spine, a ring, your own hands, or, if nothing is near, a tree outside a childhood home. Look at the wear, the softness, the scratches, and what it has been through with you. See whether something like fondness comes, the way it came for Seneca once he stopped scolding.

447.title: Each day a whole life
447.hook: treat each day as if it were a complete life
447.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism review each evening as if the day were a whole life, tying up what they can, and greet the next morning as a gift.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was platanus, the plane tree Seneca planted and grew old with. Your line was we grew old together.

Most days don't feel complete. They feel like episodes in a long series: a lot of setup, some unfinished business, and to be continued at the bottom. Most nights end with half the plot still hanging. The second half of Seneca's twelfth letter flips that feeling. What if each day were not an episode, but the whole show? To make it stick, he tells a very strange story about a Roman governor's dinner parties.
screen: `TO BE CONTINUED.` → `WHAT IF IT WERE THE WHOLE SHOW?` → `EACH DAY A WHOLE LIFE.`

segments.voice: Life is made of parts, Seneca says, like circles inside circles. A whole life is the biggest. Inside it are the years, the months, and at the center the smallest circle, a single day, with its own beginning and end, its morning and evening. He quotes the old philosopher Heraclitus: one day is equal to every day. So every day should be arranged as if it were the last in the line, as if it rounded off and completed our life. Not in a panic. In order. Then the strange story. A Roman official named Pacuvius, who governed Syria for years, held a kind of funeral for himself every evening. After dinner, with wine and ceremony, he had himself carried from the table to bed while his servants chanted, in Greek: he has lived, he has lived. Seneca admits Pacuvius did it out of bad habits. But let's do it, he says, from a good conscience. When we go to sleep, let's be able to say gladly: I have lived. And the best part: if tomorrow comes, take it as a bonus. Whoever can say I have lived gets up each morning to a gain. This isn't gloom. A day that's whole doesn't need tomorrow to rescue it, and a tomorrow that arrives anyway is pure gift, unwrapped at sunrise.

448.title: More in imagination
448.hook: we suffer more in imagination than in reality
448.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism question a fear before acting on it: is it present, is it certain, and is it truly bad?

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Pacuvius, whose servants chanted: he has lived. Your line was a whole life. Today ends a week.

Your boss sends a message at four forty-five on a Friday: can we talk Monday? That's all. No subject. By Saturday morning you've lived through the whole meeting a dozen times. You've been criticized, demoted, let go. You've drafted your defense. Then on Monday it turns out she wanted to ask which conference room you like. Two days of suffering for something that never happened. Seneca's thirteenth letter catches this habit in a single sentence.
screen: `CAN WE TALK MONDAY?` → `A WHOLE WEEKEND OF DREAD.` → `MORE IN IMAGINATION.`

segments.voice: More things frighten us than actually hurt us, Seneca tells Lucilius. Then, in Gummere's translation: we suffer more often in imagination than in reality. Some things, he says, torment us more than they should. Some torment us before they should. And some torment us when they shouldn't at all. We exaggerate a trouble, we imagine one that isn't there, or we start suffering it early. So he gives a simple test. When a fear arrives, look at it closely. Is this trouble here now, or still in the future? If it's coming, is it certain, or only likely? And is it really an evil, or does it just feel like one? Much of what we dread, he says, never arrives. Between now and then, a lot can change. Look at this week: one is enough. All mine is with me. As if seen. Cato. We grew old together. A whole life. And now, more in the mind. One thread runs through them: much of what weighs on us lives in our heads, not in the world, and the world is often kinder than our forecasts. That's not a promise that nothing bad will happen. Seneca had real troubles, and some arrived. It's a habit: check the fear against the facts before you suffer it in full.
screen: `MORE FRIGHTENS US THAN HURTS US.` · `TOO MUCH, TOO SOON, OR FOR NOTHING.` · `HERE NOW? CERTAIN? REALLY BAD?` · `THE WEEK: CHECK THE FORECAST.` · then, large: `MORE IN THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Bring one worry to mind and ask Seneca's questions slowly: is it happening now or later, certain or only possible, and how bad would it really be? Notice how much of the worry lived in the forecast. Then come back to your breath and your chair, where nothing has happened yet.
Opinione. Latin for in opinion: we suffer more often in opinion than in fact, so check each fear against the facts. Today's word.
Your line: more in the mind. Often the meeting is about conference rooms. Another week, done.

original.note: Latin: we suffer more often in opinion than in fact, from Seneca's thirteenth letter.

what a scholar hears: the Latin says opinione, by opinion, the same Stoic idea as Epictetus: it's our judgments about things that trouble us.
